https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/11.conclusion: QI has not been able to find the precise quotation displayed on the shirt in the writings of Ayn Rand. QI thinks the statement was probably derived from the dialog in a scene in "The Fountainhead". It roughly corresponds to the sentiment expressed by Howard Roark, a fictional character created by Rand.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/15.title: Quote Origin: It Is the Best Play I Ever Slept Through - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/15.quote: It Is the Best Play I Ever Slept Through
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/15.conclusion: QI has not located this jape in the writings of Oscar Wilde. However, there is evidence that he employed it. In addition, one of Wilde's biographers named Arthur Pinero as the target of the barb. The jest has evolved over time, and a version was also used by Will Rogers.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/17.title: Quote Origin: History Does Not Repeat Itself. The Historians Repeat One Another - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/17.quote: History Does Not Repeat Itself. The Historians Repeat One Another
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/17.conclusion: both of these sayings are proverbial and no precise ascription is currently known. It is reasonable to make weaker claims, e.g., Max Beerbohm popularized the adage:

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/22.title: Quote Origin: Drawing on My Fine Command of Language, I Said Nothing - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/22.quote: Drawing on My Fine Command of Language, I Said Nothing

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/24.title: Quote Origin: He Who Would Pun Would Pick a Pocket - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/24.quote: He Who Would Pun Would Pick a Pocket
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/24.conclusion: the earliest known published anecdote in 1722 ascribed the saying to the critic John Dennis. The original remark condemned one particular pun and not all puns, but the version denouncing all puns is sharper and more memorable. Alexander Pope helped to popularize a simplified and concise version of the saying, but he credited the words to Dennis.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/28.title: Quote Origin: Let Us Make a Special Effort to Stop Communicating with Each Other, So We Can Have Some Conversation - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/28.quote: Let Us Make a Special Effort to Stop Communicating with Each Other, So We Can Have Some Conversation
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/28.conclusion: QI believes that the quotation originated with Judith Martin writing as Miss Manners. The expression was slightly simplified and ultimately reassigned to Mark Twain. It is possible that the generation of the incorrect ascription was facilitated by the placement of Martin's quote adjacent to a quote ascribed to Mark Twain.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30.title: Quote Origin: I Only Write When Inspiration Strikes. Fortunately It Strikes at Nine Every Morning - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30.quote: I Only Write When Inspiration Strikes. Fortunately It Strikes at Nine Every Morning
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30.conclusion: the earliest evidence found by QI points to William Faulkner as the originator of this entertaining comment, but the support is not strong because it is indirect, and it appeared a few years after the death of Faulkner. Herman Wouk was an important locus for popularization, but he disclaimed credit.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/01.title: Quote Origin: Some People Never Miss an Opportunity to Miss an Opportunity - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/01.quote: Some People Never Miss an Opportunity to Miss an Opportunity
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/01.conclusion: the earliest evidence in 1922 pointed to George Bernard Shaw as creator of this quip although QI has not yet located any direct evidence in his writings or transcribed speeches. The phrasing has evolved over time, and in recent decades Abba Eban has been a locus for the remark's popularization.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/03.title: Quote Origin: You Can Get Much Further with a Kind Word and a Gun than with a Kind Word Alone - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/03.quote: You Can Get Much Further with a Kind Word and a Gun than with a Kind Word Alone
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/03.conclusion: QI hypothesizes that this quip was crafted by the humorist Professor Irwin Corey by 1953. Further, QI believes that Corey fabricated the ascription to Al Capone by 1969 to enhance the comical effect and with no real intention to deceive. Nevertheless, the attribution was taken seriously, and today the expression is often incorrectly attributed to Capone.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/05.title: Quote Origin: They're Cheering Us Both, You Because Nobody Understands You, and Me Because Everybody Understands Me - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/05.quote: They're Cheering Us Both, You Because Nobody Understands You, and Me Because Everybody Understands Me
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/05.conclusion: the strongest and earliest evidence for this incident known to QI appeared in the 1933 article by Charlie Chaplin. The quotation about fame was ascribed to Albert Einstein's son. QI does not know whether credit should be given to Hans Albert Einstein or Eduard Einstein.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/06.title: Quote Origin: If You Haven't Got It, You Can't Show It. If You Have Got It, You Can't Hide It - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/06.quote: If You Haven't Got It, You Can't Show It. If You Have Got It, You Can't Hide It
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/06.conclusion: this expression was used by Zora Neale Hurston in her autobiography "Dust Tracks on a Road" in 1942. In modern times the wording of the statement is sometimes slightly altered.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/08.title: Quote Origin: Don't Bend; Don't Water It Down; Don't Try to Make It Logical; Don't Edit Your Own Soul According to the Fashion - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/08.quote: Don't Bend; Don't Water It Down; Don't Try to Make It Logical; Don't Edit Your Own Soul According to the Fashion
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/08.conclusion: QI believes that the quotation should be credited to Anne Rice and not to Franz Kafka. Rice wrote the words in the foreword to a collection of stories by Kafka. She was presenting her conjectural thoughts about Kafka's attitude toward writing.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/10.title: Quote Origin: What Is the Difference Between a Misfortune and a Calamity? - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/10.quote: What Is the Difference Between a Misfortune and a Calamity?
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/10.conclusion: based on current evidence this joke template originated in France. "The Leeds Mercury" and "Punch" were loci for its popularization in the United Kingdom. The variability of the tale suggests to QI that deliberate modifications were made to conform to current events and to the political preferences of the teller.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/12.title: Quote Origin: Reorganizing is a Wonderful Method for Creating the Illusion of Progress while Actually Producing Confusion, Inefficiency, and Demoralization - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/12.quote: Reorganizing is a Wonderful Method for Creating the Illusion of Progress while Actually Producing Confusion, Inefficiency, and Demoralization
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/12.conclusion: this quotation should be credited to Charlton Ogburn Jr. and not to Petronius. Ogburn wrote two distinct but similar versions. One was printed in Harper's Magazine in January 1957 and the other appeared in his memoir "The Marauders" in 1959.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/14.title: Quote Origin: Believe Those Who Are Seeking the Truth; Doubt Those Who Find It - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/14.quote: Believe Those Who Are Seeking the Truth; Doubt Those Who Find It
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/14.conclusion: QI believes that André Gide should be credited with the statements in French and English that are cited above. His remarks were widely disseminated and influenced other writers and thinkers.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/16.title: Quote Origin: We Can Complain Because Rose Bushes Have Thorns, or Rejoice Because Thorn Bushes Have Roses - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/16.quote: We Can Complain Because Rose Bushes Have Thorns, or Rejoice Because Thorn Bushes Have Roses
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/16.conclusion: the earliest evidence found by QI for this type of saying appeared in French in a book by Alphonse Karr who declined to give an ascription. Hence, this saying has no known originator though Karr was the primal locus of popularization. The attribution to Lincoln occurred very recently and is unsupported.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/18.title: Quote Origin: Hit 'Em Hard, They'll Land Somewhere - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/18.conclusion: Stewart Maiden should be credited with this advice, and the version in September 1928 is the earliest known to QI . Bobby Jones was the primary popularizer of the maxim, and the details of his anecdote shifted over time, but the advice was unchanging.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/20.title: Quote Origin: There Are Two Kinds of People, Those Who Do the Work and Those Who Take the Credit - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/20.quote: There Are Two Kinds of People, Those Who Do the Work and Those Who Take the Credit

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/22.title: Quote Origin: 'Dog Bites a Man' Is Not News. 'Man Bites a Dog' Is News - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/22.quote: 'Dog Bites a Man' Is Not News. 'Man Bites a Dog' Is News
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/22.conclusion: the earliest instance of this adage located by QI was spoken by a fictional journalist in an 1899 book by a Pulitzer-prize-winning dramatist named Jesse Lynch Williams. It is conceivable that Lynch crafted the phrase, but QI thinks it is more likely that he was repeating an existing saying.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/26.title: Quote Origin: I Had to Get Up to Answer the Phone Anyway - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/26.quote: I Had to Get Up to Answer the Phone Anyway
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/26.conclusion: QI believes this line was probably used by Yogi Berra, but the joke was already in circulation before it was connected to Yogi. The humorous reply was credited to Desi Arnaz in a newspaper column in 1942 and that is currently the first citation located by QI .

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/28.title: Quote Origin: I Have Been Laid Up With Intentional Flu - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/28.quote: I Have Been Laid Up With Intentional Flu
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/28.conclusion: there is some evidence that this malapropism was spoken by Goldwyn; however, it is also possible that this was an existing joke that was simply reassigned to Goldwyn. QI believes that the latter option is the most likely.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/30.title: Quote Origin: Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/30.quote: Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/11/30.conclusion: QI believes that Henri Peyre deserves credit for originating this striking metaphor by 1944. He applied it to movies and radio and not TV. By 1955 John Mason Brown adapted the metaphor to television. However, he did not credit himself with the coinage; instead, he ascribed to words to an unknown young person.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/02.title: Quote Origin: If You Can't Convince Them, Confuse Them - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/02.quote: If You Can't Convince Them, Confuse Them
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/02.conclusion: the adage was in circulation by 1919. Currently, the earliest use in print was from the pen of A. C. Wilson. Harry Truman helped to popularize the expression when he used it in a speech in 1948, but he was not endorsing the approach outlined by the maxim. He was criticizing it.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/04.title: Quote Origin: The Strength of the Sole Leather Has Passed into the Fibre of Your Body - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/04.quote: The Strength of the Sole Leather Has Passed into the Fibre of Your Body
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/04.conclusion: Ralph Waldo Emerson did write a version of this adage in one of his journals in 1851. He also told it to his son who recorded it in a memoir published in 1888. Most modern instances have slightly modified the original wording.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/06.title: Quote Origin: “I Insured My Voice for $1,000,000.” “Wonderful! What Did You Do with the Money?” - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/06.quote: “I Insured My Voice for $1,000,000.” “Wonderful! What Did You Do with the Money?”
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/06.conclusion: QI believes that this tale probably began as a humorous fictional tale. The connection to Miriam Hopkins was established years after the joke entered circulation. In the earliest instances the lampooned singer was male and not female.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/09.title: Quote Origin: A Ship in Harbor Is Safe, But that Is Not What Ships Are Built For - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/09.quote: A Ship in Harbor Is Safe, But that Is Not What Ships Are Built For
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/09.conclusion: QI believes that John A. Shedd should be credited with the quotation he employed in the 1928 volume "Salt from My Attic". Grace M. Hopper did use the expression, and she helped to popularize it, but she did not coin it. The connection to Albert Einstein appeared late and was not substantive.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/19.title: Quote Origin: There Was a Young Lady Named Bright Whose Speed Was Far Faster Than Light - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/19.quote: There Was a Young Lady Named Bright Whose Speed Was Far Faster Than Light
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/19.conclusion: QI believes that Buller was the most likely composer of this limerick. The words were attributed to him by 1927, and his 1937 letter was credible. Also, QI has found no substantive counter-claims.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/21.title: Quote Origin: What You Are Comes To You - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/21.quote: What You Are Comes To You
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/21.conclusion: QI has located no substantive evidence that the quotation presented by the questioner was used by Ralph Waldo Emerson. However, the phrase was used by Norman Vincent Peale adjacent to an excerpt from an 1841 essay by Emerson. QI believes that the phrase was mistakenly reassigned directly to Emerson.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/23.title: Quote Origin: We Don't Know Who Discovered Water, But We Know It Wasn't a Fish - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/23.quote: We Don't Know Who Discovered Water, But We Know It Wasn't a Fish
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/23.conclusion: Marshall McLuhan did use a version of this saying in speeches by 1966, but he credited "someone" or "a wit". The underlying idea can be expressed in many ways. Albert Einstein employed a version of the idea in a 1936 essay, and Clyde Kluckhohn wrote an instance in 1949.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/26.title: Quote Origin: I Know Only Two Tunes: One of Them Is Yankee Doodle, and the Other Isn't - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/26.quote: I Know Only Two Tunes: One of Them Is Yankee Doodle, and the Other Isn't
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/26.conclusion: the earliest evidence suggests an anonymous origin for this jest. There is testimony that Grant, Lincoln, and Gilbert each told a version though the humorous remark was already in circulation. The evidence is not ideal because it comes from the long-term memories of individuals and was published after the deaths of these luminaries.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/28.title: Quote Origin: The Final Test of a Gentleman: His Respect for Those Who Can Be of No Possible Service to Him - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/28.quote: The Final Test of a Gentleman: His Respect for Those Who Can Be of No Possible Service to Him
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/28.conclusion: this quotation was credited to William Lyon Phelps by July 1935. QI has not yet found this saying directly in a work written by Phelps. However, QI has found no substantive support for an alternate ascription. Hence, QI thinks it is reasonable to credit Phelps.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/30.title: Quote Origin: Youth Is When You're Allowed to Stay Up Late on New Year's Eve. Middle Age Is When You're Forced To - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/30.quote: Youth Is When You're Allowed to Stay Up Late on New Year's Eve. Middle Age Is When You're Forced To
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/12/30.conclusion: QI believes that the joke originated with ‘Senator Soaper’ who in 1958 was the fictional alter ego of the journalist Bill Vaughan.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/06.title: Quote Origin: A Verbal Contract Isn't Worth the Paper It's Written On - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/06.quote: A Verbal Contract Isn't Worth the Paper It's Written On
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/06.conclusion: based on current evidence QI believes that it is reasonable to credit Bryan O'Loghlen with this saying. Yet, the line was delivered by an anonymous figure in jokes from the same time period. Hence, it is possible the ascription was manufactured. The comedian Ed Wynn used the jest when it was already in circulation.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/23.title: Quote Origin: I Wish I Was As Sure of Any One Thing As He is of Everything - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/23.quote: I Wish I Was As Sure of Any One Thing As He is of Everything
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/23.conclusion: QI believes that Lord Melbourne should be credited with this statement, and the target of his criticism was Thomas B. Macaulay? There are several different wordings, and it is not certain which was actually used by Melbourne. Other individuals may have used the expression, but based on current evidence Melbourne has priority.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/26.title: Quote Origin: You Shall Either Die Upon the Gallows or of the Pox - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/26.quote: You Shall Either Die Upon the Gallows or of the Pox

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/28.title: Quote Origin: The Only "Ism" in which Hollywood Believes Is Plagiarism - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/28.quote: The Only "Ism" in which Hollywood Believes Is Plagiarism
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/28.conclusion: the earliest citations for this saying did not present exact quotations, so there is some uncertainty about the wording. The earliest evidence also indicated that the statement was aimed at Hollywood and not an individual writer. The ascription to Dorothy Parker appeared repeatedly, and there were no substantive rivals.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/30.title: Quote Origin: The Covers of This Book Are Too Far Apart - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/01/30.quote: The Covers of This Book Are Too Far Apart

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/01.title: Quote Origin: Fanatic: One Who Can't Change His Mind and Won't Change the Subject - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/01.quote: Fanatic: One Who Can't Change His Mind and Won't Change the Subject
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/01.conclusion: there is evidence that Winston Churchill used this quip around 1952 based on Kay Halle's book; however, the expression was already in circulation by 1943. Hence, it is unlikely that Churchill coined this joke. The ascription to Churchill was widely reported in newspapers in 1952.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/04.title: Quote Origin: Most Conversations Are Simply Monologues Delivered in the Presence of a Witness - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/04.quote: Most Conversations Are Simply Monologues Delivered in the Presence of a Witness
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/04.conclusion: this notion about conversation has been expressed in several different ways over the decades. The adage from the questioner should be credited to Margaret Millar based on the 1942 citation.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/07.title: Quote Origin: There Are Two Classes of People in the World; Those Who Divide People into Two Classes and Those Who Do Not - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/07.quote: There Are Two Classes of People in the World; Those Who Divide People into Two Classes and Those Who Do Not
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/07.conclusion: QI believes that Robert Benchley should be credited with this jest which was published in 1920. Later versions were probably derived directly or indirectly from Benchley's remark though it may have been independently recreated. The first instance with the word "dichotomies" in 1967 was given an anonymous ascription.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/11.title: Quote Origin: Rap Is Black America's TV Station - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/11.quote: Rap Is Black America's TV Station
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/11.conclusion: Chuck D did describe rap music's power of communication using a television station metaphor on multiple occasions. QI recommends using a quotation directly from an interview or his book "Fight the Power". The expression of his ideas has changed over time, and the last quotation given above from his 1997 book reflects an international perspective.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/12.title: Quote Origin: I Feel that I Am Making Daily Progress - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/12.quote: I Feel that I Am Making Daily Progress
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/12.conclusion: there is substantive evidence that Casals made a remark about making progress in 1944 when he was 67 or 68 years old as indicated by the 1946 citation. There is also good evidence that he made a similar remark circa 1957 when he was 80 years old. Viewing the film created at that time would establish the precise dialog. It also seems possible that Casals reprised the comment at a later time.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/24.title: Quote Origin: If You Are Not a Liberal at 25, You Have No Heart. If You Are Not a Conservative at 35 You Have No Brain - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/24.quote: If You Are Not a Liberal at 25, You Have No Heart. If You Are Not a Conservative at 35 You Have No Brain
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/02/24.conclusion: the earliest strong match known to QI appeared in a letter written by Anselme Batbie in 1872. Significantly, Batbie credited the remark to “Burke”, probably Edmund Burke. QI has not yet located this expression in the writings of Burke, and it is possible that Burke’s changing political behavior inspired the saying and not his words.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/01.title: Quote Origin: If I Am To Speak Ten Minutes, I Need a Week for Preparation; If an Hour, I Am Ready Now - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/01.quote: If I Am To Speak Ten Minutes, I Need a Week for Preparation; If an Hour, I Am Ready Now

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/03.title: Quote Origin: You Can't Use Up Creativity. The More You Use, The More You Have - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/03.quote: You Can't Use Up Creativity. The More You Use, The More You Have
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/03.conclusion: this quotation should be credited to Maya Angelou. She spoke it during an interview in "Bell Telephone Magazine" in 1982.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/05.title: Quote Origin: Any Fool Can Paint a Picture, But It Takes a Wise Person To Be Able To Sell It - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/05.quote: Any Fool Can Paint a Picture, But It Takes a Wise Person To Be Able To Sell It
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/05.conclusion: Samuel Butler did make a comical remark about artistic salesmanship. He wrote the statement in a notebook that was published after his death.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/11.title: Quote Origin: The Jawbone of an Ass - Quote Investigator®

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/13.title: Quote Origin: There Is No Greater Mistake than To Try To Leap an Abyss in Two Jumps - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/13.quote: There Is No Greater Mistake than To Try To Leap an Abyss in Two Jumps
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/13.conclusion: the implausible notion of crossing a chasm in two jumps has been used as a simile or metaphor for many years. Examples begin by the 1870s. David Lloyd George presented a cautionary maxim of this type in his 1933 memoirs, and he often receives credit.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/15.title: Quote Origin: The Male Libido is Like Being Chained to a Madman - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/15.quote: The Male Libido is Like Being Chained to a Madman

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/17.title: Quote Origin: Written Without Fear and Without Research - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/17.quote: Written Without Fear and Without Research
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/17.conclusion: historian Carl L. Becker used this expression by 1912, and currently he is the strongest candidate for originator known to QI . The phrase was used by other historians such as Charles A. Beard, but he placed the phrase in quotation marks indicating that he was using an existing quip.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/20.title: Quote Origin: Words and Pictures Are Yin and Yang - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/20.quote: Words and Pictures Are Yin and Yang
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/20.conclusion: Theodor Seuss Geisel did say something that closely matched the expression provided by the questioner. His precise words were reported in the "Dartmouth Alumni Magazine" in 1976.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/24.title: Quote Origin: That Is Part of the Beauty of All Literature. You Discover that Your Longings Are Universal Longings - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/24.quote: That Is Part of the Beauty of All Literature. You Discover that Your Longings Are Universal Longings
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/24.conclusion: the quotation was spoken by F. Scott Fitzgerald to Sheilah Graham according to Graham's memoir. The relationship between the two took place between 1937 and 1940. Yet, the memoir was released about two decades later in 1958. The accuracy of the statement hinges on the memory of Graham who treasured her time with the illustrious writer.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/30.title: Quote Origin: It Is the Responsibility of Every Human Being To Aspire To Do Something Worthwhile - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/30.quote: It Is the Responsibility of Every Human Being To Aspire To Do Something Worthwhile
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/30.conclusion: QI believes that the expression should not be ascribed to Albert Einstein. Evidence indicates that Armand Hammer used the words in 1988, and he can be credited. However, the remark does not sound particularly original, and an earlier similar statement may be uncovered in the future.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/31.title: Quote Origin: When in Doubt Have a Man Come Through a Door with a Gun in His Hand - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/31.quote: When in Doubt Have a Man Come Through a Door with a Gun in His Hand
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/03/31.conclusion: in 1950 Raymond Chandler did write about using an armed man to move a story forward. The quotation appeared in an essay titled "The Simple Art of Murder". There were two such essays, but the quote was contained in only one. Consult the bibliographic notes below for the specifics.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/02.title: Quote Origin: Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/02.quote: Writers Are Just Schmucks with Underwoods
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/02.conclusion: the evidence in 1961 indicated that Jack Warner could be credited with calling writers "schmucks with typewriters". Yet, the citation was indirect, and the same source also ascribed the phrase "schleps with typewriters" to Warner.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/04.title: Quote Origin: Don't Tax You. Don't Tax Me. Tax That Fellow Behind the Tree - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/04.quote: Don't Tax You. Don't Tax Me. Tax That Fellow Behind the Tree
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/04.conclusion: humorous verses advocating that taxes be levied on someone "behind the tree" began to appear by the 1930s. These early instances were anonymous.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/07.title: Quote Origin: If I Had a Single Flower for Every Time I Think of You, I Could Walk Forever in My Garden - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/07.quote: If I Had a Single Flower for Every Time I Think of You, I Could Walk Forever in My Garden

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/21.title: Quote Origin: Never Lose an Opportunity of Seeing Anything Beautiful. Beauty is God's Handwriting - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/21.quote: Never Lose an Opportunity of Seeing Anything Beautiful. Beauty is God's Handwriting

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/22.title: Quote Origin: I Would Spend 55 Minutes Defining the Problem and then Five Minutes Solving It - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/22.quote: I Would Spend 55 Minutes Defining the Problem and then Five Minutes Solving It
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/22.conclusion: currently there is no known substantive support for the claim that Albert Einstein made one of these remarks. https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/24.title: Quote Origin: The Enemy of Art Is the Absence of Limitations - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/24.quote: The Enemy of Art Is the Absence of Limitations

The precise wording is uncertain, but QI recommends the version given by Jaglom in 1992. Perhaps stronger direct evidence will be uncovered by future researchers. https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/06/03.title: Quote Origin: You Don't Owe Prettiness to Anyone - Quote Investigator®

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/06/14.quote: Briefest Correspondence: Question Mark? Exclamation Mark!

Over the decades the location of the saying moved from automobiles, to coats, to flying saucers, to offices, and to graveyards.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/10/26.title: Quote Origin: Creativity Is Allowing Yourself to Make Mistakes. Art Is Knowing Which Ones to Keep - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/10/26.quote: Creativity Is Allowing Yourself to Make Mistakes. Art Is Knowing Which Ones to Keep
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/10/26.conclusion: QI believes that this quotation should be ascribed to Scott Adams. The actor comedian Ricky Gervais has employed the expression; however, he has credited Scott Adams. The incorrect attribution to Douglas Adams was constructed due to a confusion caused by the shared last name Adams.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/04.title: Quote Origin: Easy Writing's Vile Hard Reading - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/04.conclusion: QI believes that Richard Brinsley Sheridan should be credited with the couplet disseminated in 1772. The attribution to Lord Byron was apparently based on a misreading of his 1818 work "Beppo". There is substantive evidence that Hemingway spoke the adage after it was already in circulation.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/05.title: Quote Origin: Easy Reading Is Hard Writing - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/05.conclusion: QI would provisionally credit Thomas Hood with the version of the maxim he used in 1837. Yet, it is certainly possible that future researchers will locate earlier instances. This entry provides a snapshot of what is currently known by QI .

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/08.title: Quote Origin: What Is Written Without Effort Is In General Read Without Pleasure - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/08.quote: What Is Written Without Effort Is In General Read Without Pleasure

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/12.title: Quote Origin: What I Hate About Writing Is the Paperwork - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/12.quote: What I Hate About Writing Is the Paperwork
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/12.conclusion: Peter De Vries can be credited with the remark he made in the 1964 citation. The version of the joke in the 1977 compilation has become the most popular; however, QI has, to date, been unable to find substantive evidence that De Vries employed the 1977 version.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/14.title: Quote Origin: Education Is the Inculcation of the Incomprehensible Into the Ignorant by the Incompetent - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/14.quote: Education Is the Inculcation of the Incomprehensible Into the Ignorant by the Incompetent
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/14.conclusion: evidence beginning in 1933 indicated that Josiah Stamp was the key locus in the popularization of this saying, but his book titled "Ideals of a Student" used quotation marks indicating that the expression was already being disseminated. In addition, Stamp expressed disagreement with its import.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/24.title: Quote Origin: Relativity: A Hot Stove and A Pretty Girl - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/24.quote: Relativity: A Hot Stove and A Pretty Girl
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/11/24.conclusion: QI believes Einstein probably did present a version of this saying to a secretary, and she communicated it to reporters by 1929. By the 1930s Helen Dukas was acting as Einstein's intermediary, and she probably employed the expression. The oft repeated evidence is indirect.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/01.title: Quote Origin: Animal Rights and Beings from Another Planet - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/01.quote: Animal Rights and Beings from Another Planet
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/01.conclusion: the statement in the 1972 citation should be credited to John Harris. In QI's opinion, the linkage to Shaw is spurious, and it was constructed via a misinterpretation of a passage in a 1979 essay by Brigid Brophy.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/06.title: Quote Origin: Give the People What They Want and They'll Come - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/06.quote: Give the People What They Want and They'll Come
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/06.conclusion: QI suggests that George Jessel should be credited with this quip. The joke may have been retold when Harry Cohn died and when Louis B. Mayer died, but the remark was already in circulation.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/08.title: Quote Origin: It Is the Artists of This World, the Feelers and Thinkers, Who Will Ultimately Save Us - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/08.quote: It Is the Artists of This World, the Feelers and Thinkers, Who Will Ultimately Save Us
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/08.conclusion: Leonard Bernstein did speak about the unique importance of artists in society who are able to articulate and "shout the big dreams". QI suggests using the text in the nearly contemporaneous 1970 citation or the 1982 collection.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/09.title: Quote Origin: A Shortage of Sand in the Sahara - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/09.quote: A Shortage of Sand in the Sahara
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/09.conclusion: this saying has an anonymous origin. A precursor appeared in 1951 and a strong match was presented by William F. Buckley Jr. in a 1971 book although he disclaimed authorship of the joke. The early instances were about communist governments, and the quip evolved over time. In 1980 Milton Friedman published a simplified instance.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/11.title: Quote Origin: Nothing is More Unfair than to Judge the Men of the Past by the Ideas of the Present - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/11.quote: Nothing is More Unfair than to Judge the Men of the Past by the Ideas of the Present
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/11.conclusion: Barbara Tuchman was referring D.A. Winstanley who believed that it was unfair to judge historical figures by future standards of behavior and value.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/13.title: Quote Origin: They Riot in the Streets Inflamed with Wild Notions; Their Morals Are Decaying - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/13.quote: They Riot in the Streets Inflamed with Wild Notions; Their Morals Are Decaying
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/13.conclusion: QI has not yet found any substantive citations for Plato. The words have only been traced back to 1967, but the provenance remains mysterious to QI . Perhaps future researchers may discover additional clues.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/17.title: Quote Origin: A Rainy Day, Lost Luggage, and Tangled Christmas Tree Lights - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/17.quote: A Rainy Day, Lost Luggage, and Tangled Christmas Tree Lights
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/17.conclusion: QI believes that the remark about rainy days, luggage, and Christmas lights was crafted by an unnamed person who was 52 years old. The precise text appeared in the 1991 citation. The linkage to Maya Angelou was spurious.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/26.title: Quote Origin: This Just Shows What God Could Do If He Had Money - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/26.quote: This Just Shows What God Could Do If He Had Money

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/30.title: Quote Origin: Lord Northcliffe Killed the Penny Dreadful by the Simple Process of Producing a Ha'Penny Dreadfuller - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/30.quote: Lord Northcliffe Killed the Penny Dreadful by the Simple Process of Producing a Ha'Penny Dreadfuller
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/12/30.conclusion: A.A. Milne did write the remark with the clever term "ha'penny dreadfuller" in a 1948 article in "The Sunday Times". Milne was discussing the publisher Alfred Harmsworth who was elevated to the peerage and ultimately raised to Viscount Northcliffe. Hence, he was sometimes referred to as Lord Northcliffe.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/05.title: Quote Origin: Niagara Falls: The First Great Disappointment in Married Life - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/05.quote: Niagara Falls: The First Great Disappointment in Married Life
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/05.conclusion: Oscar Wilde did craft a line about underwhelmed visitors to Niagara Falls. QI believes that the two 1883 citations and the 1906 citation are all reasonable choices. The variant joke with the phrase "second greatest disappointment" was not constructed by Wilde though QI thinks it was probably derived from his remark.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/11.title: Quote Origin: The Golden Rule: Whoever Has the Gold Makes the Rules - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/11.quote: The Golden Rule: Whoever Has the Gold Makes the Rules
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/11.conclusion: QI believes that this joke can be credited to the team who crafted the "Wizard of Id" comic strip on May 3, 1965. Johnny Hart was the main gag writer in 1965 though others provided some suggestions and material.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/16.title: Quote Origin: Those Who Love Deeply Never Grow Old - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/16.quote: Those Who Love Deeply Never Grow Old
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/16.conclusion: Arthur Wing Pinero should be credited with the lines he wrote for his 1897 play "The Princess and The Butterfly". Presenting the quotation using both standard spelling and nonstandard spelling would probably be helpful.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/19.title: Quote Origin: The Eternal Stars Shine Out Again, So Soon As It Is Dark Enough - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/19.quote: The Eternal Stars Shine Out Again, So Soon As It Is Dark Enough
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/19.conclusion: we may say, with Carlyle, when it grows dark enough we can see stars.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/21.title: Quote Origin: A Gentleman Is a Man Who Never Gives Offense Unintentionally - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/21.quote: A Gentleman Is a Man Who Never Gives Offense Unintentionally
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/21.conclusion: this joke was being disseminated by 1899, and the earliest instances were anonymous. QI conjectures that the quip was constructed deliberately and was not the product of an error. Indeed, the 1920 tale in "Punch" of a printing blunder was probably an embellishment of the jest.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/23.title: Quote Origin: Every Ambitious Would-Be Empire Clarions It Abroad That She Is Conquering the World to Bring It Peace - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/23.quote: Every Ambitious Would-Be Empire Clarions It Abroad That She Is Conquering the World to Bring It Peace
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/23.conclusion: the statement under investigation has been attributed to three people: George S. Boutwell, Henry David Thoreau, and Taylor Caldwell. This confusion is unsurprising because the words appeared in a bestselling book by Taylor Caldwell in 1968. A fictional character attributed the words to Boutwell. In addition, the passage contained an embedded quotation that was attributed to Thoreau.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/26.title: Quote Origin: People Who Say It Cannot Be Done Should Not Interrupt Those Who Are Doing It - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/26.quote: People Who Say It Cannot Be Done Should Not Interrupt Those Who Are Doing It

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/29.title: Quote Origin: Melancholy Is the Pleasure of Being Sad - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/29.quote: Melancholy Is the Pleasure of Being Sad
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/01/29.conclusion: Victor Hugo should be credited with this statement which was originally constructed in French by 1866. A few different translations into English have been produced.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/01.title: Quote Origin: You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/01.quote: You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/05.title: Quote Origin: An Exclamation Point Is Like Laughing at Your Own Joke - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/05.quote: An Exclamation Point Is Like Laughing at Your Own Joke
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/05.conclusion: the advice about exclamation points in the 1958 citation was attributed to F. Scott Fitzgerald by Sheilah Graham. She published it almost two decades after the death of Fitzgerald in 1940. Nevertheless, QI believes it is reasonable to credit Fitzgerald with the comment.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/07.title: Motto Origin: The Buck Stops Here - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/07.quote: Motto Origin: The Buck Stops Here
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/07.conclusion: the motto appeared on the desk of a U.S. military officer in 1929, but the officer was unnamed, and the creator of the expression remains unknown.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/10.title: Quote Origin: It Ain’t Over ’Til the Fat Lady Sings - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/10.quote: It Ain’t Over ’Til the Fat Lady Sings

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/12.title: Quote Origin: You Can't Depend On Your Eyes When Your Imagination Is Out of Focus - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/12.quote: You Can't Depend On Your Eyes When Your Imagination Is Out of Focus
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/12.conclusion: Mark Twain wrote two intriguing quotations that differed by a single word. One was printed in his popular novel "A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court", and the other was handwritten in one of his private journals.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/17.title: Quote Origin: She Is Too Fond of Books, and It Has Turned Her Brain - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/17.quote: She Is Too Fond of Books, and It Has Turned Her Brain
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/17.conclusion: the quotation in the 1873 citation is the correct one. The saying with "addled her brain" is entertaining but inaccurate.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/21.title: Quote Origin: Only One Who Attempts the Absurd Is Capable of Achieving the Impossible - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/21.quote: Only One Who Attempts the Absurd Is Capable of Achieving the Impossible
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/21.conclusion: the original version of the adage was written in Spanish by Miguel de Unamuno who should receive credit. Different translations into English are possible including the one in 1925.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/24.title: Quote Origin: Unless You Try To Do Something Beyond What You Have Already Mastered, You Will Never Grow - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/24.quote: Unless You Try To Do Something Beyond What You Have Already Mastered, You Will Never Grow
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/24.conclusion: the passage in the 1945 citation should be credited to Ronald E. Osborn. The linkage of the saying to Ralph Waldo Emerson occurred many years after his death and the supporting evidence is not substantive.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/28.title: Quote Origin: Shoot Them Now, While They're Happy - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/28.quote: Shoot Them Now, While They're Happy
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/02/28.conclusion: Dorothy Parker did compose an astringent warning to nascent writers which appeared in "Esquire" in 1959.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/02.title: Quote Origin: The Most Exciting Phrase in Science Is Not ‘Eureka!’ But ‘That’s Funny’ - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/02.quote: The Most Exciting Phrase in Science Is Not ‘Eureka!’ But ‘That’s Funny’
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/02.conclusion: the ascription to Isaac Asimov remains uncertain. He received credit in 1987 while he was still alive. The attribution appeared in the “fortune” program of the UNIX operating system. The quotation has not yet been found in the writings, interviews, or speeches of Asimov. An interesting precursor occurred in an article by Gordon Rattray Taylor in 1965.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/09.title: Quote Origin: Good Girls Keep Diaries; Bad Girls Don't Have the Time - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/09.quote: Good Girls Keep Diaries; Bad Girls Don't Have the Time
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/09.conclusion: QI believes this quip should be ascribed to Tallulah Bankhead. The phrasing was variable and the words did not appear in an interview or speech, but there was no other substantive rival attribution.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/11.title: Quote Origin: My Ancestors Didn't Come Over on the Mayflower. They Were Just Standing There When It Docked - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/11.quote: My Ancestors Didn't Come Over on the Mayflower. They Were Just Standing There When It Docked
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/11.conclusion: this quip was circulating without attribution by 1914, and Will Rogers did employ it by 1926. QI does not know if Rogers crafted the joke or simply popularized it. Future researchers may be able to push these dates further back and provide additional insights.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/13.title: Quote Origin: To Fulfill a Dream, To Be Allowed to Sweat over Lovely Labor, To Be Given the Chance To Create, Is the Meat and Potatoes of Life. The Money Is the Gravy - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/13.quote: To Fulfill a Dream, To Be Allowed to Sweat over Lovely Labor, To Be Given the Chance To Create, Is the Meat and Potatoes of Life. The Money Is the Gravy
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/13.conclusion: the statement Bette Davis made in her 1962 autobiography has provided stimulation to others. QI suggests using the text printed in the 1962 book.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/15.title: Quote Origin: He Who Laughs, Lasts - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/15.conclusion: the earliest instance known to QI appeared in a poem by W. E. Nesom in 1917, and it was possible that he crafted this quip. The second earliest instance was written by George F. Worts in 1926. This version was more concise. Mary Pettibone Poole helped to popularize the joke, but she did not construct it.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/21.title: Quote Origin: Sometimes I'm Terrified of My Heart, of Its Constant Hunger for Whatever It Is It Wants - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/21.quote: Sometimes I'm Terrified of My Heart, of Its Constant Hunger for Whatever It Is It Wants
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/21.conclusion: QI believes that the passage should be ascribed to the musical artist Poe and not Edgar Allan Poe.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/26.title: Quote Origin: Some Writers Are Only Born to Help Another Writer to Write One Sentence - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/26.quote: Some Writers Are Only Born to Help Another Writer to Write One Sentence
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/26.conclusion: Hemingway did make an acerbic remark about one writer providing another writer with one sentence. The original phrasing was given in the 1935 citation. Other instances have evolved over the decades.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/28.title: Quote Origin: Your Bald Head Feels as Smooth as My Wife's Cheek - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/28.quote: Your Bald Head Feels as Smooth as My Wife's Cheek
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/03/28.conclusion: tracing this quip has been difficult because of the fragmentary and probably sanitized early published evidence. The first person linked to the tale was someone named S. H. Hale in 1924. The rejoinder was spoken by an unidentified barber shop customer.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/04.title: Quote Origin: When Two Men in Business Always Agree, One of Them Is Unnecessary - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/04.quote: When Two Men in Business Always Agree, One of Them Is Unnecessary
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/04.conclusion: QI suggests that William Wrigley Jr. should be credited with the words recorded in "The American Magazine" in 1931. QI further suggests that the saying should not be assigned to Ezra Pound or Henry Ford.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/06.title: Quote Origin: To Repeat What Others Have Said, Requires Education; To Challenge It, Requires Brains - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/06.quote: To Repeat What Others Have Said, Requires Education; To Challenge It, Requires Brains
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/06.conclusion: Mary Pettibone Poole included this saying in her 1938 compilation. At this time QI knows of no earlier evidence and suggests that the words should be ascribed to Poole.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/11.title: Quote Origin: Definition of Freedom: It's Being Easy in Your Harness - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/11.quote: Definition of Freedom: It's Being Easy in Your Harness
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/11.conclusion: Robert Frost did speak about freedom in 1954. His remark did not conform to a simple freestanding quotation; instead, the most natural template was question-response.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/14.title: Quote Origin: I Think that I Shall Never See a Billboard Lovely as a Tree - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/14.quote: I Think that I Shall Never See a Billboard Lovely as a Tree
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/14.conclusion: QI believes that the work should be credited to Ogden Nash. He released two versions; one was printed in "The New Yorker" in 1932, and another appeared in "The Face is Familiar" in 1940. Select the version you like the best.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/16.title: Quote Origin: Chance Is the Nickname of Providence - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/16.quote: Chance Is the Nickname of Providence

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/18.title: Dialogue Origin: “She Is Always Kind to Her Inferiors” “But Where Does She Find Them?” - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/18.quote: “She Is Always Kind to Her Inferiors” “But Where Does She Find Them?”
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/18.conclusion: this joke was linked to Dorothy Parker by 1937. The initial target of mockery was an anonymous actress. The version aimed at Clare Boothe Luce emerged by 1941, but the primary supporting passage in "The New Yorker" was not very convincing because the chronology offered was inconsistent.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/20.title: Quote Origin: Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/20.quote: Chance, Coincidence, Miracles, Pseudonyms, and God
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/20.conclusion: Albert Einstein was first linked to the quotation under examination many years after his death. There is no substantive evidence that Einstein ever employed the saying.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/24.title: Quote Origin: No Bastard Ever Won a War by Dying for His Country - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/24.quote: No Bastard Ever Won a War by Dying for His Country
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/24.conclusion: QI believes that George S. Patton did employ this line in more than one speech in 1943 and 1944. Precursors were already in circulation before Patton rallied Allied troops. The exact phrasing of the statement was variable, and Patton may have expressed the remark in different ways at different times.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/26.title: Quote Origin: I Had Six Theories About Bringing Up Children - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/26.quote: I Had Six Theories About Bringing Up Children
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/26.conclusion: there is no substantive support for ascribing the joke to John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester. Perhaps some other Lord Rochester or some other John Wilmot employed the quip, but QI has not yet found evidence for this.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/28.title: Quote Origin: I Would Rather Have Two Girls at 21 Each Than One At 42 - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/28.quote: I Would Rather Have Two Girls at 21 Each Than One At 42
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/28.conclusion: the vaudeville performer Great Lester used a version of this gag in 1915, but its origin was not certain. Fred Allen recorded the line when he started performing in vaudeville.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/30.title: Quote Origin: You Can Avoid Reality, But You Cannot Avoid the Consequences of Avoiding Reality - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/30.quote: You Can Avoid Reality, But You Cannot Avoid the Consequences of Avoiding Reality
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/04/30.conclusion: the target quotation has not been located in the works of Ayn Rand. She did make remarks that were thematically similar by the 1960s. Weak precursors were circulating several decades before the 1960s. In an ideal world, a quotation ascribed to an author would be taken directly from an interview or from a work created by the author.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/02.title: Quote Origin: If George Washington Were Alive Today He'd Turn Over in His Grave - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/02.quote: If George Washington Were Alive Today He'd Turn Over in His Grave
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/02.conclusion: the earliest instance of this comical line located by QI was written by William Cuffe, 4th Earl of Desart in 1879. The uneasy grave belonged to English manufacturer and free trade exponent Richard Cobden. The remark has been employed by many people during the past 136 years. However, the linkages to Samuel Goldwyn and Yogi Berra are not well supported.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/04.title: Quote Origin: Storytelling: Just Give Them Two and Two and Let Them Add It Up - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/04.quote: Storytelling: Just Give Them Two and Two and Let Them Add It Up

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/08.title: Quote Origin: All Science Is Either Physics or Stamp Collecting - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/08.quote: All Science Is Either Physics or Stamp Collecting
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/08.conclusion: this adage is usually attributed to Ernest Rutherford, and QI has found no alternative ascriptions with substantive support. The first known citation credited Rutherford, but it appeared two years after his death. John Desmond Bernal apparently was the prime locus for the dissemination of the remark and its common attribution.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/10.title: Origin of Spoonerism: You Are Occupewing My Pie - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/10.quote: Origin of Spoonerism: You Are Occupewing My Pie
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/10.conclusion: this entertaining spoonerism was attributed to Reverend William A. Spooner by 1887. However, many Spoonerisms have been concocted and assigned to Spooner over the years, and the linkages have almost always been spurious.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/12.title: Origin of Spoonerism: You Have Hissed All My Mystery Lectures - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/12.quote: Origin of Spoonerism: You Have Hissed All My Mystery Lectures
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/12.conclusion: this series of spoonerisms was in circulation by 1911. QI hypothesizes that each of these well-designed comical fragments was constructed by a student or other humorist. It was unlikely that Reverend William A. Spooner inadvertently uttered these remarks.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/14.title: Quote Origin: It's the Guy You Give Something To That You Can't Please - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/14.quote: It's the Guy You Give Something To That You Can't Please

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/23.title: Quote Origin: The Existence of Forgetting Has Never Been Proved - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/23.quote: The Existence of Forgetting Has Never Been Proved
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/23.conclusion: in 1881 Friedrich Nietzsche did write a passage that corresponded to the quotation being examined. The 1911 and 1997 translations given above did differ from the common modern statement, but the similarity was easily perceived. A scholar may wish to present a direct translation in conjunction with the original German text.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/28.title: Quote Origin: Have You Tried Curiosity? - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/28.conclusion: QI believes that Dorothy Parker originated this jest. The scenario presented by Lyons has the best evidentiary basis.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/28.title: Quote Origin: Drunk on the Idea That Love, Only Love, Could Heal Our Brokenness - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2015/05/28.quote: Drunk on the Idea That Love, Only Love, Could Heal Our Brokenness

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/06/28.quote: The Only Trouble with Capitalism Is Capitalists. They're Too Damned Greedy

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/06/30.title: Quote Origin: The Trouble with Socialism Is Socialism; the Trouble with Capitalism is Capitalists - Quote Investigator®

By 1978 he was ascribing the words to William Schlamm. QI believes that Schlamm is the top candidate for coiner of the adage. Currently, the evidence linking Winston Churchill to the statement appeared too late and is weak.

The phrase "truth and duty" was a later elaboration of the phrase which initially only mentioned "truth".

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/08/20.quote: We Are Taught To Fly in the Air Like Birds, and To Swim in the Water Like the Fishes; But How To Live on the Earth We Don't Know

Perhaps future researchers will locate a passage by Maxim Gorky discussing the quotation. Martin Luther King, Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, C. E. M. Joad, Walter Winchell, and Jack Paar all employed the saying, but only after it was in circulation.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/08/24.title: Quote Origin: If Noah Had Been Truly Wise, He Would Have Swatted Those Two Flies - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2016/08/24.quote: If Noah Had Been Truly Wise, He Would Have Swatted Those Two Flies

The ascription to Plato occurred more than 125 years ago, but no substantive support has been located.

The evidence was indirect, and it remains unclear where and when Lyell learned about the remark. The adage achieved wide distribution, and QI has found no evidence that Agassiz ever attempted to disclaim the ascription during the decade he lived after 1863.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/06/25.quote: We Cannot Direct the Wind, But We Can Adjust the Sails

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/06.quote: Don't Wrestle with a Chimney Sweep or You Will Get Covered with Grime

The earliest evidence located by QI was recorded by Boswell in his "The Life of Samuel Johnson". Oxford academic William Adams spoke a version circa 1776. The metaphor was popular and used by many. In modern time, politician Tony Benn has employed it while crediting his father.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/10.title: Quote Origin: Never Attempt To Teach a Pig To Sing; It Wastes Your Time and Annoys the Pig - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/10.quote: Never Attempt To Teach a Pig To Sing; It Wastes Your Time and Annoys the Pig

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/12.quote: The Enormous Multiplication of Books in Every Branch of Knowledge is One of the Greatest Evils of This Age

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/14.title: Quote Origin: The Early Bird Catcheth the Worme - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/14.quote: The Early Bird Catcheth the Worme
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/14.conclusion: this saying appeared in a collection of proverbs published in 1636 titled "Remaines Concerning Britaine" by William Camden. The 1636 edition was posthumous as Camden had died in 1623.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/15.title: Quote Origin: The Worm Was Punished for Early Rising - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/15.quote: The Worm Was Punished for Early Rising
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/15.conclusion: John Godfrey Saxe should be credited with the quip about the early worm being punished, and Frederick Locker-Lampson should be credited with the similar joke he crafted.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/16.title: Quote Origin: You're Not the Customer; You're the Product - Quote Investigator®
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/16.quote: You're Not the Customer; You're the Product
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/16.conclusion: this saying evolved over time. Richard Serra and Carlota Fay Schoolman crafted an interesting precursor in 1973. A strong match was written by Tom Johnson in 2001. An extended statement was written by Andrew Lewis in 2010.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/19.quote: If I Could Remember the Names of These Particles, I Would Have Been a Botanist
https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/19.conclusion: Enrico Fermi died in 1954. Fellow physicist Leon M. Lederman credited him with the remark in 1963. During the ensuing decades Fermi received credit many times almost exclusively. The linkage to Einstein is unsupported.

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/07/22.quote: There Is Less in This Than Meets the Eye

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/08/06.quote: I Wanted To Change the World. But I Have Found That the Only Thing One Can Be Sure of Changing Is Oneself

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2022/06/07.quote: There Are Old Traders and Bold Traders, But There Are No Old, Bold Traders

Styron acknowledged Stein while using a variant phrasing.
